title: What is Ayurveda — Origin and Definition
content: Ayurveda is one of the world's oldest holistic healing systems, originating in the Indian subcontinent more than 3,000 to 5,000 years ago. The word 'Ayurveda' is derived from two Sanskrit roots: 'Ayu' meaning 'life' or 'longevity', and 'Veda' meaning 'knowledge' or 'sacred science'. Together, Ayurveda translates to 'The Science of Life'. According to classical texts such as the Charaka Samhita, health (Swastha) is not merely the absence of disease, but a state of dynamic equilibrium between body, mind, spirit, and environment: 'Samadosha Samagnischa Samadhatu Malakriya Prasannatmendriyamanah Swastha Iti Abhidhiyate' (Sushruta Samhita). Health is maintained when doshas, metabolic fire (Agni), bodily tissues (Dhatus), and excretory functions (Malas) are in balanced proportion, and soul, senses, and mind are at peace.
source: CCRAS - Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences
section: Ayurveda: The Science of Life and Well-being

title: Panchamahabhuta — The Five Great Elements
content: Ayurveda posits that all matter in the universe, including the human body, is composed of the five fundamental elements known as Panchamahabhutas: 1. Akasha (Space/Ether): characterized by non-resistance, omnipresence, lightness, and subtle sound; forms body cavities and conduits. 2. Vayu (Air): characterized by mobility, dryness, coolness, and lightness; governs biological movement, nerve impulses, and breathing. 3. Tejas/Agni (Fire): characterized by heat, luminosity, transformation, and sharpness; governs digestion, metabolism, sight, and body temperature. 4. Jala/Apas (Water): characterized by fluidity, liquidity, coolness, and cohesion; provides lubrication, cytoplasm, plasma, and bodily secretions. 5. Prithvi (Earth): characterized by stability, heaviness, density, and structure; forms bones, muscles, cartilage, and teeth. Every physical substance contains all five elements in varying proportions, with one or two predominating.
source: Ministry of AYUSH — Fundamentals of Ayurveda Guidelines
section: Chapter 1: Cosmic Elements and Biological Composition

title: Tridosha Theory — Overview of the Three Bio-energies
content: The Tridosha theory is the cornerstone of Ayurvedic physiology and pathology. The five elements combine in pairs to form three dynamic bio-energetic forces called Doshas: Vata, Pitta, and Kapha. The word 'Dosha' etymologically means 'that which can become vitiated or imbalanced', but in their balanced state (Samyavastha), they sustain all physiological functions: 1. Vata (composed of Space and Air) governs all biological movement, circulation, respiration, and nervous system impulses. 2. Pitta (composed of Fire and Water) governs all metabolic transformation, biochemical reactions, digestion, body heat, and cognitive clarity. 3. Kapha (composed of Water and Earth) governs physical structure, cellular cohesion, lubrication, immunity, stability, and emotional grounding. Each individual possesses a unique proportional baseline of these three doshas formed at conception, known as Prakriti.
section: Principles of Tridosha and Biological Balance

title: Vata Dosha — Characteristics, Functions, and Qualities
content: Vata Dosha is primarily composed of Akasha (Space) and Vayu (Air). It is considered the leader of the doshas ('Pittu pangu, kapha pangu...') because Pitta and Kapha are mobile only when carried by Vata. The traditional qualities (Gunas) of Vata are: Ruksha (dry), Laghu (light), Sheeta (cold), Khara (rough), Sukshma (subtle), and Chala (mobile). Functions of balanced Vata include initiation of natural urges, sensory perception, motor activity, speech, cellular division, heart rhythm, and mental alertness. When Vata is aggravated, manifestations include dry skin, constipation, flatulence, insomnia, nervousness, cold extremities, and musculoskeletal stiffness. Vata increases during autumn, late afternoon (2 PM to 6 PM), after digestion, and in the elder stage of life.

title: Pitta Dosha — Characteristics, Functions, and Qualities
content: Pitta Dosha is primarily composed of Tejas (Fire) and Jala (Water). It governs all thermogenesis, biochemical transformations, enzymatic action, and cognitive processing. The classical qualities (Gunas) of Pitta are: Sasneha (slightly unctuous/oily), Teekshna (sharp/penetrating), Ushna (hot), Laghu (light), Visra (fleshy odor), Sara (flowing/spreading), and Drava (liquid). Functions of balanced Pitta include robust digestion (Pachana), optical visual acuity, maintenance of normal body temperature, healthy complexion, intelligence, courage, and discernment. When Pitta is vitiated, manifestations include acid indigestion, heartburn, excessive sweating, inflammatory conditions, skin irritations, irritability, and loose stools. Pitta naturally peaks during summer, midday (10 AM to 2 PM), midnight, mid-digestion, and youth.

title: Kapha Dosha — Characteristics, Functions, and Qualities
content: Kapha Dosha is formed from Jala (Water) and Prithvi (Earth). It provides structural foundation, anatomical stability, tissue lubrication, and biological resilience (Bala). The classical qualities (Gunas) of Kapha are: Guru (heavy), Sheeta (cold), Mridu (soft), Snigdha (unctuous/oily), Madhura (sweet), Sthira (stable), and Pichchila (slimy/cohesive). Functions of balanced Kapha include lubrication of joints (Sandhibandha), immunity (Ojas generation), cellular cohesion, strength, patience, forgiving temperament, and endurance. When Kapha is elevated, symptoms include lethargy, excessive sleepiness, slow digestion, congestion, heaviness, fluid retention, and weight gain. Kapha naturally peaks in late winter and spring, in the morning (6 AM to 10 AM), evening (6 PM to 10 PM), and childhood.

title: Prakriti and Vikriti — Constitution vs. Imbalance
content: In Ayurveda, Prakriti refers to an individual's unique biological constitution established at the moment of conception (Shukra-Shonita Samyoga), influenced by parental genetics, maternal diet and mental state, and seasonal factors. Prakriti remains essentially constant throughout a person's lifetime and determines physical build, digestive tendency, psychological disposition, and disease vulnerability. The primary categories are Vataja, Pittaja, Kaphaja, dual-dosha combinations (Vata-Pitta, Pitta-Kapha, Vata-Kapha), and balanced tridoshic (Samadosha). In contrast, Vikriti denotes the current state of doshic imbalance resulting from inappropriate diet, lifestyle, climate changes, psychological stress, or age. The educational objective of Ayurveda is to recognize deviations from one's baseline Prakriti and restore balance through gentle dietary and lifestyle adjustments.
source: CCRAS — Clinical & Research Methodology in Ayurveda

title: Agni — The Digestive and Metabolic Fire
content: Agni represents the biological fire responsible for digestion, absorption, assimilation, and transformation of food and experiences. According to Charaka, 'Rogah sarve api mande agnau'—all somatic diseases originate from impaired Agni. Ayurveda describes thirteen types of Agni: 1. Jatharagni (the master digestive fire in the gastrointestinal tract); 2. Five Bhutagnis (elemental metabolic fires transforming nutrients according to the 5 elements); 3. Seven Dhatvagnis (tissue-specific metabolic fires responsible for synthesizing each of the seven bodily tissues). There are four clinical states of Jatharagni: Sama Agni (balanced digestion), Vishama Agni (irregular, fluctuating digestion associated with Vata), Tikshna Agni (hyperactive, sharp digestion associated with Pitta), and Manda Agni (sluggish, slow digestion associated with Kapha). Protecting Agni is the primary preventative directive in Ayurveda.

title: Ama — Endogenous Metabolic Toxins
content: Ama literally translates to 'unripe', 'undigested', or 'uncooked'. When digestive fire (Jatharagni) is compromised, ingested food is not properly metabolized. Instead, it ferments and produces an unassimilated, foul-smelling, sticky metabolic byproduct called Ama. Ama clogs the micro-circulatory channels (Srotas), interferes with cellular communication, and combines with vitiated doshas to initiate pathology (Samadosha). Classical signs of Ama accumulation include: feeling of heaviness (Gaurava), chronic fatigue and lassitude, coated tongue with bad breath, constipation or irregular sticky stools, loss of appetite, and mental fogginess. Traditional management focuses on Deepana (stimulating digestive fire) and Pachana (metabolizing Ama through light diet, warm water, and digestive spices like dry ginger and cumin).

title: Sapta Dhatus — The Seven Bodily Tissues
content: Ayurveda describes human anatomy in terms of seven structural and physiological tissues termed Sapta Dhatus, which nourish each other sequentially: 1. Rasa (Plasma/lymph): sustains hydration and nutrition ('Preenana'); 2. Rakta (Blood/erythrocytes): imparts color, vitality, and oxygenation ('Jeevana'); 3. Mamsa (Muscle tissue): envelops bone and executes movement ('Lepana'); 4. Meda (Adipose/fat tissue): lubricates body parts and buffers temperature ('Sneha'); 5. Asthi (Bone tissue): provides physical framework and protects vital organs ('Dharana'); 6. Majja (Bone marrow and nervous tissue): fills bone cavities and facilitates nerve conduction ('Poorana'); 7. Shukra (Reproductive tissue/vital essence): enables fertility and cellular regeneration ('Garbhotpadana'). The refined subtle essence of all seven healthy Dhatus is called Ojas.

title: Srotas, Malas, and Ojas — Channels, Wastes, and Vital Immunity
content: Three foundational physiological concepts in Ayurveda complete systemic understanding: 1. Srotas (Micro and Macro Channels): conduits through which nutrients, waste, and bio-energies circulate. Classical texts identify major internal systems including Pranavaha (respiratory), Annavaha (digestive), and Udakavaha (fluid regulation) srotas. 2. Malas (Excretory Metabolic Byproducts): bodily wastes whose prompt excretion maintains systemic purity: Purisha (feces), Mutra (urine), and Sweda (perspiration). Balanced waste formation and evacuation are vital for preventing auto-intoxication. 3. Ojas: the purest, most refined biological essence derived from the completion of tissue synthesis (Dhatu Paka). Ojas represents primary systemic immunity (Vyadhikshamatva), cellular resilience, sensory clarity, and radiant vitality.
